thesis: A machine learning model that learned from 2019's lightning says Alaska could get more than double, up to nearly seven times, today's ground strikes under high emissions, and the honest read is a range: even its floor matters in a state where lightning fires burn nearly all the acres, while its ceiling is the question its own authors taught us to ask, will it hold outside the conditions it trained on.
falsifiability: False if a test outside the training conditions (the test the authors' preprint calls for, c21) shows this model does no better than a simple training-average benchmark (what the preprint found for the ML models it tested, c20), because then even the floor would carry no skill. Also false in its first half if the floor were not more than double (c8 says +116%), or if lightning were a minor cause of Alaska's burned acres (c23 says at least 93% every year 2015 to 2024).
supporting_facts: The mechanism: an XGBoost model trained on lightning and weather observations from 2019 (c3, c4), six everyday weather readings (c5), ground strikes on a half-degree grid (c6). Run on today's climate most of Alaska got under one bolt per sq km a year (c7).

The number is a range: Alaska +116% to +594% under high emissions, per AGU (c8), the top nearly sevenfold (c9), against the world's +76% to +140% (c10). The Alaska range is much wider than the world's (our arithmetic on c8 and c10, never the study's claim, never explained).

The stakes are Alaska's: lightning fires burned at least 93% of wildfire acres every year 2015 to 2024 (c23), about 3.1 million acres in 2022 (c24). The study didn't model fire (c25), so fire is context, kept apart from the projection.
counterpoint_to_honor: Two fair cases, each a scene. The method question at full strength: the model learned from one year (c3); run backward it gives about 12% per degree (c11, c12), inside earlier studies' 8 to 17% (c14), but forward it gives about 30% (c13), and the release says the gap is mostly different math (c14); Krause was 'quite surprised' (c15) and names 'quite a large uncertainty' (c16); a month earlier Krause and Rammig's preprint found a simple training-average benchmark beat the ML lightning models it tested and warned scores can overstate projection skill (c19, c20, c21). Never said to have tested this model, never says the sensitivity causes the width. The model's defense, shown straight: it beat a regression and three existing formulas (c22), and separate work already found boreal lightning ignitions rising since 1975 (c27).
valence_defense: ML does real work here and points at the thing that lights nearly all of Alaska's fires, so doom is wrong and dismissal is wrong. It's an unvalidated high-emissions projection whose authors flag their own field's evaluation limits, so celebration would oversell it. The film shows what the range is made of and lets the floor land.
who_it_serves: Alaskans who live with lightning-fire summers, Alaska fire and land managers, the legislators who fund suppression, and Alaska researchers placed to run the outside-the-training-data test.
second_movement: The recontextualising fact is the October 17th preprint by two of the same authors: test scores can overstate projection skill, test models outside their training conditions. It turns the film from 'a scary number' into 'a number that comes with its own test', and the button asks who should run that test.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst A: Alaska gets a gridded projection of its main fire igniter and should use the range as a planning envelope
runner_ups.why_lost: 'never had' is unsupported (earlier projections exist, r1), and 'planning envelope' skips the preprint's warning; kept as the closing question.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst B: the stretch of the range rides a sensitivity jump from 12 to 30 percent per degree
runner_ups.why_lost: no claim says the sensitivity causes the range's width, and it left out the Alaska fire stakes; kept as the Act 3 methods scene.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst C: the width is the finding, treat 'more than double' as the floor and 'nearly 7x' as an open question
runner_ups.why_lost: the core survived as the synthesis, but 'rests on a sensitivity' was an unsupported causal link and the range must always be given whole.
